[MATH: |x + 1||= 2x − 4;|5 + 1||= 2(5) − 4;|6||= 10 − 4; 6|= 6✓]
Since [MATH: x=5] satisfies the original equation, it's a valid solution.
- If [MATH: |x + 1|=-(x + 1),] we obtain
[MATH: |x + 1||= 2x − 4; − (x + 1)|= 2x − 4; − x − 1|= 2x − 4; − 1|= 3x − 4; 3|= 3x; 1|= x; x|= 1.]
This potential solution is valid only if it solves the original equation. So, let's plug it back in:
[MATH: |x + 1||= 2x − 4;|1 + 1||= 2(1) − 4;|2||= 2 − 4; 2|= − 2×]
Since [MATH: x=1] does not satisfy the original equation, it's not a valid solution. It's called an extraneous solution.

  • If [MATH: |2x-3|=-(2x-3),] we obtain [MATH: |2x − 3||= − x + 1; − (2x − 3)|= − x + 1; − 2x + 3|= − x + 1; 3|= x + 1; 2|= x; x|= 2.] This potential solution is valid only if it solves the original equation. So, let's plug it back in: [MATH: |2x − 3||= − x + 1;|2(2) − 3||= − (2) + 1;|4 − 3||= − 2 + 1;|1||= − 1; 1|= − 1×] Since [MATH: x=2] does not satisfy the original equation, it's not a valid solution.

Therefore, our equation has no solutions.

sections.normalized_html: Solve the equation [MATH: |2x +5| - 4x = 1.]
sections.readable_text: Solve the equation [MATH: |2x +5| - 4x = 1.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We start by isolating the absolute value on the left-hand side:

[MATH: |2x + 5|− 4x|= 1;|2x + 5||= 4x + 1]

Now, we have two cases:

  • If [MATH: |2x + 5|=2x+ 5,] we obtain [MATH: |2x + 5||= 4x + 1; 2x + 5|= 4x + 1; 5|= 2x + 1; 4|= 2x; x|= 2.] This potential solution is valid only if it solves the original equation. So, let's plug it back in: [MATH: |2x + 5||= 4x + 1;|2(2) + 5||= 4(2) + 1;|4 + 5||= 8 + 1;|9||= 9; 9|= 9✓] Since [MATH: x=2] satisfies the original equation, it's a valid solution.

  • If [MATH: |2x+5|=-(2x+5),] we obtain [MATH: |2x + 5||= 4x + 1; − (2x + 5)|= 4x + 1; − 2x − 5|= 4x + 1; − 5|= 6x + 1; − 6|= 6x; x|= − 1.] This potential solution is valid only if it solves the original equation. So, let's plug it back in: [MATH: |2x + 5||= 4x + 1;|2(− 1) + 5||= 4(− 1) + 1;|− 2 + 5||= − 4 + 1;|3||= − 3; 3|= − 3×] Since [MATH: x=-1] does not satisfy the original equation, it's not a valid solution.

Therefore, the solution of our equation is [MATH: x = 2.]

items.title: Finding Points of Intersection

sections.normalized_html: Find the points of intersection of [MATH: y = \vert 2x+1 \vert] and [MATH: y = -3x+11.]
sections.readable_text: Find the points of intersection of [MATH: y = \vert 2x+1 \vert] and [MATH: y = -3x+11.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The [MATH: x]-coordinates of the intersection points correspond to solutions of the equation

[MATH: |2x+1| = -3x+11.]

Now, we have the following two cases:

  • For the branch with a negative slope, where [MATH: |2x+1| = -(2x+1)], we obtain [MATH: |2x + 1||= − 3x + 11; − (2x + 1)|= − 3x + 11; − 2x − 1|= − 3x + 11; x − 1|= 11; x|= 12.] This potential solution is valid only if it solves the original equation. So, let's plug it back in: [MATH: |2x + 1||= − 3x + 11;|2(12) + 1||= − 3(12) + 11;|24 + 1||= − 36 + 11;|25||= − 25; 25|= − 25×] Since [MATH: x=12] does not satisfy the original equation, it is not the [MATH: x]-coordinate of a point of intersection.

  • For the branch with a positive slope, where [MATH: |2x+1| = 2x+1], we obtain [MATH: |2x + 1||= − 3x + 11; 2x + 1|= − 3x + 11; 5x + 1|= 11; 5x|= 10; x|= 2.] This potential solution is valid only if it solves the original equation. So, let's plug it back in: [MATH: |2x + 1||= − 3x + 11;|2(2) + 1||= − 3(2) + 11;|4 + 1||= − 6 + 11;|5||= 5; 5|= 5✓] Since [MATH: x=2] satisfies the original equation, it is an [MATH: x]-coordinate of a point of intersection.

So, the [MATH: x]-coordinate of the point of intersection is [MATH: x=2.]

Finally, we can find the [MATH: y]-coordinate of the intersection point by substituting our solution back into either of the curves. Let's use the line [MATH: y=-3x+11 \mathbin{:}]

[MATH: y|= − 3x + 11; = − 3(2) + 11; = − 6 + 11; = 5]

Therefore, the point of intersection has coordinates [MATH: (2,5).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let's now consider the following equation:
[MATH: \vert x + 1 \vert = 2x - 4]

Content:
Geometrically, solving this equation gives us the [MATH: x]-coordinate of the point of intersection [MATH: P] of the curves [MATH: y = |x+1|] and [MATH: y=2x-4.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/eb1265b74d69192bc48f8bbb2b4634c6]

Content:
Let's now discuss how to find the intersection point algebraically.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: A Worked Example

Content:
We wish to find the solution to the equation

Content:
[MATH: \vert x + 1 \vert = 2x - 4.]

Content:
For this equation to be true, either the positive or negative of the expression inside the absolute value must be equal to the right-hand side of the equation.

Content:
Therefore, we have the following two cases:

Content:
[MATH: |x+1| = x+1 \qquad \textrm{and}\qquad |x+1| = -(x+1)]

Content:
We now consider these two cases separately:

Content:
- If [MATH: |x + 1|=x + 1,] we obtain the following equation:
[MATH: x+1 = 2x-4]
We now solve this equation using the usual methods:
[MATH: x + 1|= 2x − 4; 1|= x − 4; 5|= x; x|= 5]
This potential solution is valid only if it solves the original equation. So, let's plug it back in:
[MATH: |x + 1||= 2x − 4;|5 + 1||= 2(5) − 4;|6||= 10 − 4; 6|= 6✓]
Since [MATH: x=5] satisfies the original equation, it's a valid solution.
- If [MATH: |x + 1|=-(x + 1),] we obtain
[MATH: |x + 1||= 2x − 4; − (x + 1)|= 2x − 4; − x − 1|= 2x − 4; − 1|= 3x − 4; 3|= 3x; 1|= x; x|= 1.]
This potential solution is valid only if it solves the original equation. So, let's plug it back in:
[MATH: |x + 1||= 2x − 4;|1 + 1||= 2(1) − 4;|2||= 2 − 4; 2|= − 2×]
Since [MATH: x=1] does not satisfy the original equation, it's not a valid solution. It's called an extraneous solution.

Content:
Therefore, the only solution of our equation is [MATH: x = 5.] This solution corresponds to the point [MATH: P,] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0245f6dda01d9e9a49323fc33b913fa5]

Content:
Watch out! Whenever we want to solve an absolute value equation where the variable is on both sides, we must always check that the solutions satisfy the original equation.

Content:
Some absolute value equations have no solutions at all! Let's see an example.

---

Item 3 — Example: Solving Absolute Value Equations With Extraneous Solutions

Example Prompt:
Solve the equation [MATH: \vert 2x-3 \vert = -x+1.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We have the following two cases:

- If [MATH: |2x-3|=2x-3,] we obtain
[MATH: |2x − 3||= − x + 1; 2x − 3|= − x + 1; 2x|= − x + 4; 3x|= 4; x|= (4)/(3).]
This potential solution is valid only if it solves the original equation. So, let's plug it back in:
[MATH: |2x − 3||= − x + 1;|2 ⋅ (4)/(3) − 3||= − ((4)/(3)) + 1;|(8)/(3) − 3||= − (4)/(3) + 1;|(8)/(3) − (9)/(3)||= − (4)/(3) + (3)/(3);|− (1)/(3)||= − (1)/(3); (1)/(3)|= − (1)/(3)×]
Since [MATH: x=-\dfrac 43] does not satisfy the original equation, it's not a valid solution.
- If [MATH: |2x-3|=-(2x-3),] we obtain
[MATH: |2x − 3||= − x + 1; − (2x − 3)|= − x + 1; − 2x + 3|= − x + 1; 3|= x + 1; 2|= x; x|= 2.]
This potential solution is valid only if it solves the original equation. So, let's plug it back in:
[MATH: |2x − 3||= − x + 1;|2(2) − 3||= − (2) + 1;|4 − 3||= − 2 + 1;|1||= − 1; 1|= − 1×]
Since [MATH: x=2] does not satisfy the original equation, it's not a valid solution.

Therefore, our equation has no solutions.

Item 6 — Example: Isolating an Absolute Value

Example Prompt:
Solve the equation [MATH: |2x +5| - 4x = 1.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We start by isolating the absolute value on the left-hand side:

[MATH: |2x + 5|− 4x|= 1;|2x + 5||= 4x + 1]

Now, we have two cases:

- If [MATH: |2x + 5|=2x+ 5,] we obtain
[MATH: |2x + 5||= 4x + 1; 2x + 5|= 4x + 1; 5|= 2x + 1; 4|= 2x; x|= 2.]
This potential solution is valid only if it solves the original equation. So, let's plug it back in:
[MATH: |2x + 5||= 4x + 1;|2(2) + 5||= 4(2) + 1;|4 + 5||= 8 + 1;|9||= 9; 9|= 9✓]
Since [MATH: x=2] satisfies the original equation, it's a valid solution.
- If [MATH: |2x+5|=-(2x+5),] we obtain
[MATH: |2x + 5||= 4x + 1; − (2x + 5)|= 4x + 1; − 2x − 5|= 4x + 1; − 5|= 6x + 1; − 6|= 6x; x|= − 1.]
This potential solution is valid only if it solves the original equation. So, let's plug it back in:
[MATH: |2x + 5||= 4x + 1;|2(− 1) + 5||= 4(− 1) + 1;|− 2 + 5||= − 4 + 1;|3||= − 3; 3|= − 3×]
Since [MATH: x=-1] does not satisfy the original equation, it's not a valid solution.

Therefore, the solution of our equation is [MATH: x = 2.]

Item 9 — Example: Finding Points of Intersection

Example Prompt:
Find the points of intersection of [MATH: y = \vert 2x+1 \vert] and [MATH: y = -3x+11.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The [MATH: x]-coordinates of the intersection points correspond to solutions of the equation

[MATH: |2x+1| = -3x+11.]

Now, we have the following two cases:

- For the branch with a negative slope, where [MATH: |2x+1| = -(2x+1)], we obtain
[MATH: |2x + 1||= − 3x + 11; − (2x + 1)|= − 3x + 11; − 2x − 1|= − 3x + 11; x − 1|= 11; x|= 12.]
This potential solution is valid only if it solves the original equation. So, let's plug it back in:
[MATH: |2x + 1||= − 3x + 11;|2(12) + 1||= − 3(12) + 11;|24 + 1||= − 36 + 11;|25||= − 25; 25|= − 25×]
Since [MATH: x=12] does not satisfy the original equation, it is not the [MATH: x]-coordinate of a point of intersection.

- For the branch with a positive slope, where [MATH: |2x+1| = 2x+1], we obtain
[MATH: |2x + 1||= − 3x + 11; 2x + 1|= − 3x + 11; 5x + 1|= 11; 5x|= 10; x|= 2.]
This potential solution is valid only if it solves the original equation. So, let's plug it back in:
[MATH: |2x + 1||= − 3x + 11;|2(2) + 1||= − 3(2) + 11;|4 + 1||= − 6 + 11;|5||= 5; 5|= 5✓]
Since [MATH: x=2] satisfies the original equation, it is an [MATH: x]-coordinate of a point of intersection.

So, the [MATH: x]-coordinate of the point of intersection is [MATH: x=2.]

Finally, we can find the [MATH: y]-coordinate of the intersection point by substituting our solution back into either of the curves. Let's use the line [MATH: y=-3x+11 \mathbin{:}]

[MATH: y|= − 3x + 11; = − 3(2) + 11; = − 6 + 11; = 5]

Therefore, the point of intersection has coordinates [MATH: (2,5).]
